title: Divide and Conquer
tagline: Split the problem in half, solve each half recursively, combine the results — and watch O(n²) brute-force collapse to O(n log n).

sections.content:
Divide and conquer is a **recursive algorithm design paradigm** built on three steps: **Divide** the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type, **Conquer** each subproblem recursively (base cases solve trivially), and **Combine** the subproblem solutions into the solution for the original problem. The paradigm is powerful because splitting in half at each level produces a logarithmic depth of recursion — O(log n) levels — and if the combine step is efficient, total work is O(n log n) rather than O(n²).

Classic examples include merge sort (divide: split array; conquer: sort each half; combine: merge), quicksort (divide: partition around pivot; conquer: sort each side; combine: trivial), binary search, quickselect (find k-th smallest in expected O(n)), and Strassen's matrix multiplication. The **master theorem** gives a closed-form complexity for the recurrences these algorithms produce, making analysis systematic rather than ad hoc.

sections.title: Counting Votes in a City
sections.content:
Imagine counting votes from a city of one million ballots. Counting sequentially takes forever. Instead, split the city into two districts of 500k, then each district into two regions of 250k, and so on — down to precincts of a manageable size. Each precinct counts its own ballots (base case). Results bubble back up: combine two precinct totals into a region total, two region totals into a district total, and finally two district totals into the city total.

The *combination* step at each level is trivial — just addition. The recursive splitting means the work is done at log n levels of the hierarchy. This is merge sort applied to vote tallies: split, solve, merge. The key insight is that a hard problem on n items becomes two easy problems on n/2 items, each of which become two easier problems on n/4 items — until the base case is trivially solvable.

**Recurrence relations** capture divide-and-conquer complexity formally. Merge sort's recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): two subproblems of half the size, combined in O(n) time (the merge). Binary search is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1): one subproblem of half the size, O(1) to compare and decide direction. Quickselect's average recurrence is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n): one subproblem of expected half the size after partitioning.

**The master theorem** solves recurrences of the form T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d) where a ≥ 1, b > 1, d ≥ 0. There are three cases based on comparing a (branching factor) with b^d (work per level times branching effect): if log_b(a) > d, the recursion tree is bottom-heavy and T(n) = O(n^(log_b a)); if log_b(a) = d, each level does equal work and T(n) = O(n^d · log n); if log_b(a) < d, the tree is top-heavy and T(n) = O(n^d). Merge sort: a=2, b=2, d=1 — log_2(2)=1=d — case 2 — T(n) = O(n log n). Binary search: a=1, b=2, d=0 — log_2(1)=0=d — case 2 — T(n) = O(log n).

**Quickselect** finds the k-th smallest element in expected O(n) without sorting. It partitions the array around a pivot (O(n)) and recurses on only the relevant partition — not both. On average the pivot lands near the median, halving the problem. Worst-case (always picking max/min as pivot) degrades to O(n²), which randomised pivot selection avoids in expectation.

**The combine step is critical.** If combination costs O(n²), divide and conquer offers no advantage over brute force. Merge sort's O(n) merge is efficient. Strassen's matrix multiplication improves the combine to reduce the branching factor from 8 to 7, dropping complexity from O(n³) to O(n^2.807) — a non-obvious but significant improvement for large matrices.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: mergeSort splits the array in half at each level (O(log n) levels) and merges in O(n) per level — total O(n log n). The merge step's two-pointer walk is the key combine operation. quickselect partitions in O(n) but recurses on only one partition (unlike quicksort which does both), achieving expected O(n) total — it finds the k-th smallest without sorting the entire array.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Write the recurrence before you code.** Before implementing a divide-and-conquer algorithm, explicitly state T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n): how many subproblems (a), what fraction of size (1/b), and how expensive is the combine step (f(n)). Then apply the master theorem to verify you're achieving a better complexity than brute force. If the combine step is O(n²), dividing in half only saves a constant factor — the algorithm is still O(n²). The O(n) merge in merge sort is what makes it O(n log n) rather than O(n²).

items: Divide and conquer has three phases: **Divide** (split into subproblems), **Conquer** (recurse on each), and **Combine** (merge results) — correctness follows from induction on the recursive structure.
The **master theorem** solves T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d) in three cases based on comparing log_b(a) with d — balanced (O(n^d log n)), bottom-heavy (O(n^(log_b a))), or top-heavy (O(n^d)).
**Merge sort** runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space — the O(n) merge step at log n levels gives O(n log n). It is **stable** and preferred when stability matters.
**Quickselect** finds the k-th smallest element in expected O(n) by partitioning and recursing on **one** side only — unlike quicksort which recurses on both.
The **combine step determines the algorithm's power** — an O(n) combine at O(log n) levels gives O(n log n); an O(n²) combine gives no improvement over brute force despite the recursion.

quiz.question: What are the three phases of a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
options: Initialise, iterate, terminate
Divide, conquer, combine
Search, compare, swap
Partition, recurse, memoize
quiz.explanation: Divide and conquer has three phases: Divide (split the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type), Conquer (solve each subproblem recursively — base cases solve directly), and Combine (merge subproblem solutions into the solution for the original problem).

quiz.question: What recurrence describes merge sort's time complexity?
quiz.explanation: Merge sort divides into 2 subproblems of size n/2 (so a=2, b=2), and the merge step costs O(n) per level (d=1). The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). By the master theorem, log_2(2)=1=d, so T(n) = O(n log n).

quiz.question: Applying the master theorem to T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) — which case applies and what is the result?
options: Bottom-heavy (log_b a > d) → O(n)
Balanced (log_b a = d) → O(log n)
Top-heavy (log_b a < d) → O(1)
The master theorem does not apply here
quiz.explanation: Here a=1, b=2, d=0. log_2(1) = 0 = d — this is the balanced case. Master theorem gives T(n) = O(n^d · log n) = O(1 · log n) = O(log n). This is binary search — one subproblem of half the size, O(1) work per level, O(log n) levels.

quiz.question: How does quickselect differ from quicksort in its recursive structure?
options: Quickselect uses a min-heap; quicksort uses in-place partitioning
Quickselect recurses on only ONE partition after pivot placement; quicksort recurses on BOTH
Quickselect is always O(n log n); quicksort is O(n) average
Quickselect requires a sorted input; quicksort works on any input
quiz.explanation: After partitioning around a pivot, quicksort recurses on both the less-than and greater-than partitions (sorting both). Quickselect only needs the k-th element — after partitioning, it recurses on only the partition that contains index k. This halves the expected work per level: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n) expected, versus O(n log n) for full sort.

quiz.question: What is the key reason merge sort achieves O(n log n) rather than O(n²)?
options: It divides the array into exactly 2 halves
The merge (combine) step runs in O(n) using a two-pointer technique rather than O(n²)
It uses O(log n) stack frames
It avoids comparing elements across different halves
quiz.explanation: The divide into halves creates O(log n) levels. If each combine step were O(n²), total cost would be O(n² log n). The two-pointer merge is O(n) per level — scanning both sorted halves simultaneously in linear time. This O(n) combine multiplied by O(log n) levels gives O(n log n).

quiz.question: What is the worst-case complexity of quickselect, and what causes it?
options: O(n log n) — when the array is nearly sorted
O(n²) — when the pivot is always the minimum or maximum element
O(n log² n) — when the recursion depth exceeds log n
O(n) always — randomised pivot guarantees linear time
quiz.explanation: If the pivot is always the minimum or maximum, the partition is completely unbalanced: one side has n-1 elements and the other has 0. Quickselect then recurses on n-1 elements, then n-2, then n-3 — T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) = O(n²). Randomised pivot selection makes this worst case extremely unlikely, achieving expected O(n).

quiz.question: Strassen's algorithm for n×n matrix multiplication uses recurrence T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²). What is its complexity via the master theorem?
options: O(n²)
O(n² log n)
O(n³)
quiz.explanation: a=7, b=2, d=2. log_2(7) ≈ 2.807 > 2 = d — bottom-heavy case. T(n) = O(n^(log_2 7)) = O(n^2.807). Naive matrix multiplication has a=8, b=2, d=2 — log_2(8)=3>2 — giving O(n^3). Strassen reduces the subproblem count from 8 to 7, dropping complexity by about O(n^0.19).

quiz.question: The 'count inversions' algorithm augments merge sort to count pairs (i,j) where i<j but arr[i]>arr[j]. When during merge does an inversion get counted?
options: When two equal elements are compared
When an element from the right half is taken before remaining elements in the left half — each remaining left element forms an inversion with it
When the array is initially divided into halves
After the merge completes, by scanning the merged array
quiz.explanation: During the merge, if right[j] < left[i], then right[j] is also less than left[i], left[i+1], ..., left[end] (since left is sorted). Each of those constitutes an inversion with right[j]. Adding (left.length - i) inversions at this moment counts all split inversions — inversions where one element comes from the left half and the other from the right.

quiz.question: Which property distinguishes divide and conquer from dynamic programming?
options: Divide and conquer always runs faster than DP
Divide and conquer subproblems are independent (no overlap); DP subproblems overlap and caching is needed
DP uses recursion; divide and conquer uses iteration
Divide and conquer requires sorted input; DP does not
quiz.explanation: In divide and conquer (merge sort, binary search), each subproblem is solved exactly once — subproblems don't overlap. In DP (Fibonacci, knapsack), the same subproblem is needed by multiple higher-level subproblems — overlap makes caching worthwhile. Without overlapping subproblems, DP's memoisation provides no benefit over plain recursion.

quiz.question: For merge sort, what is the space complexity and why?
options: O(1) — it sorts in-place like quicksort
O(n log n) — each level of recursion copies the full array
O(n) — auxiliary arrays for merging, though only O(n) total space is live at once
O(log n) — only the recursion stack is counted
quiz.explanation: Each merge operation creates a temporary array to hold the merged result. At any point in the recursion, the total space across all active merge operations on the call stack is O(n) — not O(n log n) — because sibling subproblems don't overlap in time (one completes before the other starts). The call stack itself is O(log n). Total space: O(n).
